messages.content: When must voter registration stop before an election?
The Commission must stop registration at least 90 days before any election. This requirement is stated in Section 9(6) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s9-0].
In what formats must the National Register of Voters be kept?

The Commission must keep the Register of Voters in electronic format in its central database and in manual, printed, paper-based format. This is required by Section 9(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s9-0].
What documents can a person present to register as a voter under continuous registration?

For continuous registration, a person must appear in person with a Nigerian birth certificate, a Nigerian passport, or a National Identification Number (NIN). This requirement is in Section 10(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s10-0].
When a general election is announced, which voters' register is used for that election?
The official voters' register for a general election is the current Register of Voters certified by the Commission. Section 10(4) of the Electoral Act, 2026 requires this [act-s10-0].
Can registration officers be members of political parties?
Officers appointed for voter registration must not belong to any political party. This is mandated by Section 11(1) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s11-0].
What happens if a voter does not object to a registration officer during the registration process?
A voter’s failure to object to a registration officer does not make the register invalid. Section 11(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026 states this rule [act-s11-0].
What are the basic qualifications for a person to be registered as a voter?

To be registered, a person must be a Nigerian citizen, be 18 years or older, and be ordinarily resident, work in, and originate from the Local Government, Area Council or Ward of the registration centre, and must appear for registration. Section 12(1) of the Electoral Act, 2026 sets these qualifications [act-s12-0].
What is the penalty for registering more than once in the same registration centre?

A person who registers more than once in the same centre may be fined at least N100,000, imprisoned for at least one year, or receive both penalties. This penalty is set out in Section 12(3) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s12-0].
I moved to a different constituency before the election. Can I still vote there?

Yes, you can apply to be entered on the Transferred Voters List if you are resident in a polling area of the new constituency and are registered elsewhere. You must submit a copy of your voters' card and make the application not later than 90 days before the date of an election in that constituency. The Resident Electoral Commissioner will decide whether to add your name to the list. [act-s13-0]
What does the electoral officer do after my name is added to the Transferred Voters List?

After your name is entered on the Transferred Voters List, an electoral officer assigns you to a polling station or polling area in the constituency and indicates the assignment in the list. The officer then issues you a new voters' card and retrieves your previous card. A copy of the entry is sent to the electoral officer of the constituency. [act-s13-0]
What information must I provide when registering as a voter?

When registering, the registration officer must demand the information needed to confirm that you are qualified to be registered according to the Act. This information allows the officer to ascertain your eligibility [act-s14-0].
If I cannot read or write, can someone else fill out my registration form?

Yes, if you are illiterate or disabled, the registration officer may complete the application form on your request. This helps you meet the registration requirement without needing to read or write. [act-s14-0]
How can I obtain a certified copy of the voters' register for my state?

You can obtain a certified true copy of the voters' register for your state by applying to the Commission. The copy may be for the whole State, a Local Government, an Area Council, or specific polling units or registration areas. [act-s15-0]
Do I have to pay to get a copy of the voters' register?

Yes, you must pay the fees that the Commission determines to obtain a certified copy of the voters' register. The fees are set by the Commission and are required before the copy is issued. [act-s15-0]
Is it allowed to have more than one voters' card?
No, a voter shall not hold more than one valid voters' card. Holding more than one card violates subsection (2) of the Act. [act-s16-0]
What penalty do I face if I hold more than one voters' card?

If you hold more than one valid voters' card, you commit an offence and may be fined up to N500,000, imprisoned for up to one year, or both. The penalty applies upon conviction by a court. [act-s16-0]
What must I do if I lose my voter's card before the election?

If a voter's card is lost, destroyed, defaced, torn or otherwise damaged, the owner must apply in person to the electoral officer or any authorised officer not less than 90 days before polling day, stating the circumstances [act-s18-0]. The owner may also print a downloadable copy.
Can I receive a replacement voter's card less than 90 days before polling day, and what are the penalties if someone issues it?

A replacement permanent voter's card may not be issued to any voter less than 90 days before polling day. Anyone who issues a replacement in violation of this rule commits an offence. The offence carries a fine of up to N200,000, imprisonment for up to two years, or both, as set out in the Act [act-s18-0].
When will the Commission display the voters' register for public scrutiny?

The Commission must display the voters' register for public scrutiny not later than 90 days before a general election. The display period lasts seven days and the register is shown at each registration area and on the Commission's website [act-s19-0].
How long do I have to raise an objection to my name being omitted or included in the voters' register?
After the register is displayed, any person may raise an objection within 14 days of the display. The objection must be submitted on the form prescribed by the Commission [act-s19-0].
Who can hear my claim about a missing name on the voters list?

The Commission may appoint a Revision Officer to hear and determine claims and objections about entries in or omissions from the preliminary list of voters. This officer can also appoint assistants as needed [act-s20-0].
If I disagree with the Revision Officer's decision, where can I appeal and is the decision final?

If a person is dissatisfied with the Revision Officer's determination, they may appeal within seven days to the Resident Electoral Commissioner for that State. The Resident Electoral Commissioner's decision is final under the Act [act-s20-0].
What are the penalties for selling my voter's card?

Selling a voter's card is an offence under the Act. The offender is liable to a fine of not less than N5,000,000, imprisonment for not less than two years, or both. Additionally, the offender is not eligible to stand for election in Nigeria for at least 10 years [act-s22-0].
If I am caught buying votes, what punishment can I face?

Buying votes is an offence under the Act. The penalty is the same: a fine of not less than N5,000,000, imprisonment of not less than two years, or both, and ineligibility to run for election for at least 10 years [act-s22-0].
What punishment can a person receive for signing a voter registration form in someone else's name?
Under Section 23(1)(b) of the Electoral Act, 2026, this act is an offence liable to a fine not more than N100,000 or imprisonment for a term not more than one year, or both [act-s23-0].
What are the penalties for threatening voters to stop them from registering?

Section 23(2)(a) states that causing or inducing persons to refrain from registering by duress is an offence punishable with a fine not more than N500,000 or imprisonment for a term not more than five years [act-s23-0].
What can the Commission do if an emergency makes it impossible to hold an election on the scheduled date?

According to Section 24(2), the Commission may postpone the election and appoint another date for the holding of the postponed election, provided the reason for the postponement is cogent and verifiable [act-s24-0].
When can election results be declared after a postponed election?
Section 24(4) specifies that there shall be no return for the election until polling has taken place in the area concerned after the substituted date [act-s24-0].
Who is responsible for announcing election results at the polling unit?
Section 25(1)(a) states that the Presiding Officer at the polling unit shall announce the results of the election [act-s25-0].
At which collation centre does the returning officer declare the winner for a Presidential election?
Under Section 25(2)(g), the returning officer declares the winner at the State Collation Centre for a Presidential election [act-s25-0].
What must election officials do before taking part in an election?

Section 26(1) requires all staff, electoral officers, presiding officers, returning officers and security officials to affirm or swear to an oath of loyalty and neutrality as in the Second Schedule, not accept bribe or gratification, and perform duties impartially [act-s26-0].
What is the penalty for an election official who violates the oath of neutrality?
Section 26(2) says that a person who violates subsection (1) commits an offence punishable under section 124 of this Act [act-s26-0].
Who is prohibited from being appointed as an election officer under the Electoral Act, 2026?

No person who is a member of a political party or who has openly expressed support for any candidate shall be appointed as an election officer. This rule is in Section 27(1) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s27-0].
Which security forces may the Commission request for deployment to protect election materials and officials?

The Commission shall only request for the deployment of the Nigerian Armed Forces for the purpose of securing the distribution and delivery of election materials and protection of election officials. This is stated in Section 27(3) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s27-0].
How many days before a general election must the Commission publish the notice of election?
The Commission must publish the notice not later than 300 days before the day appointed for holding the election. This requirement is in Section 28(1) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s28-0].
What information must be included in the notice of election published by the Commission?

The notice must state the date of the election and appoint the place at which nomination papers are to be delivered. This is required by Section 28(1)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s28-0].
Within what timeframe must a political party submit its list of candidates for a general election?

Every political party must submit the list of candidates not later than 120 days before the date appointed for a general election. This is set out in Section 29(1) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s29-0].
What document must accompany the list of candidates submitted by a political party?

The list must be accompanied by an affidavit sworn to by the candidate at the Federal High Court, High Court of a State, or Federal Capital Territory, indicating that the candidate has fulfilled all constitutional requirements. This requirement is in Section 29(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s29-0].
If a court finds that a candidate's affidavit contains false information about constitutional eligibility, what is the consequence?
The court shall issue an order disqualifying the candidate and the sponsoring political party. This provision is in Section 29(6) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s29-1].
What address must a candidate provide when submitting the prescribed nomination form?

The candidate must furnish an identifiable address in the state where he or she intends to contest the election, at which all documents and court processes shall be served. This requirement is in Section 29(8) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s29-1].
What are the requirements for nominating a candidate for an election?

A candidate must be nominated in writing by such number of persons whose names appear on the register of voters in the constituency as the Commission may prescribe [act-s30-0]. A person may not nominate more than one person for the same office [act-s30-0].
What is the penalty for nominating more than one person for the same office?

A person who nominates more than one person for the same office commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a fine not more than N100,000 or imprisonment for a term of three months or both [act-s30-0]. However, the nomination is not invalidated by such action [act-s30-0].
What is the minimum number of electoral wards that a Local Government Area must have?

The Commission shall divide each Local Government Area into registration areas or Electoral Wards not being less than 10 as the circumstances may require [act-s40-0]. Therefore, a Local Government Area must have at least ten wards.
Who decides how many polling units are set up in a registration area?
The Commission shall establish an adequate number of polling units in each registration area or Electoral Ward [act-s40-0]. The Commission also allots voters to those polling units [act-s40-0].
What voting devices may be used for elections?

The Commission shall provide suitable boxes, electronic voting machine or any other voting device for the conduct of elections [act-s41-0]. The specific forms to be used are determined by the Commission [act-s41-0].
Can polling agents inspect the electoral materials before voting begins?

Polling agents who are in attendance at a polling unit may inspect originals of the electoral materials before the commencement of the election [act-s41-0]. They may record this inspection as evidence in writing, on video or by other means [act-s41-0].
How many days before an election must the Commission invite political parties to inspect their identity on ballot papers?

The Commission shall, not later than 60 days to an election, invite in writing a political party that nominated a candidate to inspect its identity on samples of electoral materials [act-s42-0]. The party then has two days to approve or disapprove its identity in writing [act-s42-0].
What happens if a political party does not respond to the Commission's invitation to inspect its identity?

If a political party fails to comply with the invitation, it shall be deemed to have approved its identity on samples of electoral materials proposed for the election [act-s42-0]. Consequently, the party cannot later complain of unlawful exclusion based on its identity [act-s42-0].
What must a candidate submit to appoint a polling agent for a polling unit?

The candidate must give a notice in writing addressed to the Resident Electoral Commissioner of the State that includes the polling agent’s name, address and contact details. The notice must be accompanied by two passport photographs and a sample signature of the polling agent and be given to the electoral officer at least 14 days before the election date [act-s43-0].
Which public officials are not allowed to serve as polling agents unless they resign three months before the election?

A person who is serving as Chairman or member of a Local Government Area or Area Council, Commissioner, Deputy Governor or Governor of a State, Minister of the Federal Government, or any other person holding elective or appointive political office under any tier of government is prohibited from serving as a polling agent. He may serve only if he has resigned from his office at least three months prior to the election [act-s43-0].
If a polling agent does not attend an act required by the Act, does that invalidate the act?

The non‑attendance of the Polling Agent at the time and place appointed for the act does not invalidate the act if the act is otherwise done properly. The same applies if the Polling Agent refuses to do the act, provided the act is performed correctly [act-s43-1].
What is the effect if a polling agent refuses to perform an act that the Act requires?
If a polling agent refuses to perform an act required by the Act, the act is not invalidated. This holds as long as the act is performed correctly by someone else [act-s43-1].
What steps must the Presiding Officer take with the ballot box before voting begins?

At the hour fixed for opening the poll, the Presiding Officer must open the empty ballot box or present the voting device and show it to persons lawfully present. He must then close and seal the box in a manner that prevents it from being opened by any unauthorised person [act-s46-0].
Where must the sealed ballot box be kept during the voting period?
The ballot box shall be placed in full view of all present. It must be kept in that condition until the close of poll [act-s46-0].
What must a voter present to be accredited before voting?

The voter must present himself to a Presiding Officer for accreditation at the polling unit in the constituency where his name is registered. He must also provide his permanent voters card (PVC) [act-s47-0].
What happens if the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System fails at a polling unit and no replacement device is provided?

If the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System or any other technological device fails in a polling unit and a fresh card reader or technological device is not deployed, the election in that unit shall be cancelled. The Commission may then schedule another election within 24 hours, but only if it is satisfied that the result of the election in that polling unit will substantially affect the final result of the whole election and declaration of a winner in the constituency concerned [act-s47-0].
How must I cast my vote according to the Electoral Act?

Voting at an election shall be by open secret ballot, and a voter must mark the ballot paper in the manner prescribed by the Commission. All ballots must be deposited in the ballot box in the open view of the public. This is required by section 50 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s50-0].
Who decides the voting procedure for elections?

The Commission determines the procedure for voting and transmission of results, subject to section 60 of this Act. This rule is set out in subsection (2) of section 50 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s50-0].
Can I vote for more than one candidate in an election?

No, a voter shall not vote for more than one candidate or record more than one vote in favour of any candidate at any one election. This prohibition is stated in subsection (1) of section 51 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s51-0].
What happens if more votes are cast in my polling unit than the number of accredited voters?

If the number of votes cast exceeds the number of accredited voters, the Presiding Officer shall cancel the result of the election in that polling unit. This requirement is found in subsection (2) of section 51 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s51-0].
Will my ballot be rejected if I have a thumb stain from the ink used at the polling station?

No, any print resulting from the staining of the thumb of the voter in the voting compartment shall not be or be deemed to be a mark of identification under this section. Therefore a thumb stain does not cause rejection of the ballot paper. This rule is in subsection (1) of section 52 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s52-0].
What type of ink must the Commission use for thumb marks on ballot papers?
The Commission shall use indelible ink for any thumb mark by voters on ballot papers. This requirement is stated in subsection (2) of section 52 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s52-0].
What should I do if I accidentally damage my ballot paper?

You may deliver the spoilt ballot paper to the Presiding Officer; if the Presiding Officer is satisfied that the ballot paper is spoilt, he or she shall issue another ballot paper to you in place of the one delivered, and the spoilt ballot paper shall be immediately marked cancelled. This procedure is set out in section 53 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s53-0].
Who decides whether a ballot paper is spoilt and can be replaced?

The Presiding Officer decides if satisfied that the ballot paper is spoilt, then issues a new ballot paper and marks the original cancelled. This authority is given by section 53 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s53-0].
Who is responsible for delivering the election results after they are announced?

According to Section 62(1) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s62-0], the Presiding Officer must deliver the recorded result together with election materials under security to the person prescribed by the Commission. The delivery must be accompanied by the candidates or their polling agents where available.
How can a voter obtain a certified copy of election results from the National Electronic Register?

Section 62(3) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s62-0] states that any person or political party may obtain a certified true copy of any election result kept in the National Electronic Register by paying the fees set by the Commission. The copy may be in printed or electronic format and can cover results for a State, Local Government, Area Council, registration area, Electoral Ward or Polling Unit.
What must a collation officer verify before announcing election results?

Section 62(4) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s62-1] requires the collation officer to verify that the number of accredited voters on the collated result matches the number recorded under section 47(2) and transmitted from polling units, and that the votes stated match the votes recorded and transmitted under section 60(4). Only after these checks may the officer announce the result.
Which voter numbers must a returning officer use when collating results?

Under Section 62(5) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s62-1], a returning officer must use the number of accredited voters recorded under section 47(2) and transmitted directly from polling units under section 60(5) to collate and announce the result, provided the collated result at his or a lower level is correct.
What documents must a returning officer review when there is a dispute over a polling unit result?

Section 62(6) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s62-2] states that the officer must review the original disputed collated result, the Smart Card Reader or other accreditation device data, the accreditation data recorded under section 47(2) and transmitted from the polling unit, and the votes and result recorded and transmitted under section 60(5). These items are used to determine the correctness of the disputed result.
If a disputed election result is found to be incorrect, what must the collation officer do?

According to Section 62(7) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s62-2], when a disputed result is found incorrect, the collation officer must re-collate and announce a new result using the information listed in subsection (6)(a) through (d). This ensures the final result reflects the verified data.
Can a ballot paper without an official mark still be counted in an election?

Section 63(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s63-0] allows a ballot paper without an official mark to be counted if the returning officer is satisfied that it came from a book of ballot papers furnished to the Presiding Officer of the polling unit for that election. In that case, the absence of the official mark does not prevent the vote from being counted.
Under what condition is a ballot paper without an official mark counted?

Section 63(2) of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s63-0] states that a ballot paper without an official mark shall be counted only when the returning officer confirms it originated from the correct book of ballot papers provided to the polling unit’s Presiding Officer for the election in question. This confirmation overrides the requirement for the official mark.
What must the Presiding Officer write on a ballot paper that is rejected?

The Presiding Officer must endorse the word rejected on the ballot paper that is rejected under section 52(1) of the Act or for any other reason. The ballot papers shall not be counted unless the returning officer overrules the Presiding Officer and allows it [act-s64-0].
What must happen if a candidate or polling agent objects to a ballot paper being rejected?

If a candidate or polling agent objects at the time the decision is made, the Presiding Officer must add the phrase but objected to after the word rejected on the ballot paper. The Presiding Officer must also prepare a statement listing the number of rejected papers, the reason for rejection and their serial numbers, and must allow the candidate or polling agent to copy that statement upon request [act-s64-0].
Under what conditions can the Commission review a declaration or return of election results?

The Commission may review a declaration or return within seven days if it receives a report from its officials and is satisfied that the declaration or return may have been made under duress or knowingly and willfully contrary to the procedures prescribed under section 62(4)–(8) of this Act. The review is carried out by the Commission as provided in Section 65 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s65-0].
How much time does the Commission have to review a declaration or return after receiving a report?
The Commission has seven days to review the declaration and return after it receives a report from its officials. This period is specified in Section 65 of the Electoral Act, 2026 [act-s65-0].
How is the winner determined in a presidential or gubernatorial election according to the Electoral Act?

In an election for President or Governor, whether contested or not, the result is ascertained by counting the votes cast for each candidate. The candidate who receives the highest number of votes is declared elected by the appropriate returning officer, subject to sections 133, 134 and 179 of the Constitution [act-s66-0].
What must happen before a candidate can be declared elected in a contested election for other offices?

For any contested election to an elective office other than President or Governor, the votes must be counted for each candidate and the result ascertained. The candidate with the highest number of votes is then declared elected by the appropriate returning officer, subject to the same constitutional provisions [act-s66-0].
What is the Commission required to do regarding election guidelines?

The Commission shall issue and publish guidelines for the elections in the Federal Government Gazette. These guidelines must include provisions for the step‑by‑step recording of the poll in the electoral forms, beginning at the polling unit and continuing to the last collation centre for the ward or constituency where the result is declared [act-s70-0].
Where does the step‑by‑step recording of the poll start and end according to the guidelines?

The recording starts at the polling unit and proceeds through each level until it reaches the last collation centre for the ward or constituency where the result is declared. The guidelines require this process to be followed so that the election result can be declared at the appropriate centre [act-s70-0].
What must a presiding officer do with the result form at the ward level according to the Electoral Act?

According to the Electoral Act, a presiding officer must stamp, sign and countersign the result form at the ward level. Copies must be given to police officers and polling agents where available [act-s71-0].
What is the penalty for a presiding officer who fails to stamp and sign a ballot paper result sheet without a lawful reason?
Such an officer commits an offence. On conviction, they face a minimum of three years imprisonment without an option of fine [act-s71-0].
What is the maximum election expense allowed for a presidential candidate under the Electoral Act, 2026?
Under the Electoral Act, 2026, the maximum election expenses for a presidential candidate are set by law. The limit is N10,000,000,000 [act-s92-0].
What is the maximum amount an individual may donate to a candidate according to the Electoral Act, 2026?
The Electoral Act, 2026 places a limit on donations to candidates. An individual may donate no more than N500,000,000 [act-s92-0].
What penalty does an accountant face if they falsify a document related to a candidate's election expenditure?

If an accountant falsifies a document about a candidate's election spending, the law treats it as an offence. The penalty is a fine of at least N5,000,000 or three years imprisonment, or both [act-s92-1].
Can an accountant be punished for helping a candidate forge a document about election donations?

An accountant who helps a candidate forge a document about election donations is also committing an offence. The same penalty applies: a fine of not less than N5,000,000 or three years imprisonment, or both [act-s92-1].
What does the Electoral Act define as "election expenses" for a political party?
The Electoral Act defines election expenses for a political party in clear terms. They are the expenses incurred from the notice date up to and including polling day for that election [act-s93-0].
What penalty may a political party face if it fails to submit its audited election expenses return on time?

A political party that does not submit its audited election expenses return on time faces financial penalties. The party may be fined up to N10,000,000 and the court may add up to N1,000,000 per day for each day after the due date until the return is submitted [act-s93-0].
What penalty does a political party face if it spends more than the allowed election expenses?
The party commits an offence and is liable on conviction to a maximum fine of N10,000,000. In addition, the Commission forfeits the amount by which the expenses exceed the limit [act-s93-1].
Where can the public view the audited returns of political parties and what details are included?

The Commission makes the audited returns available for public inspection at its headquarters and state offices during regular business hours. The returns list each contributor’s name, address, occupation, and the amount contributed [act-s93-1].
What is the minimum fine for a party that accepts a contribution exceeding the prescribed limit?
A party that breaches the contribution limit is liable to a fine of not less than N5,000,000. The excess amount must also be forfeited to the Commission [act-s94-0].
When must a party sponsoring a candidate submit its contribution report to the Commission?

The party sponsoring a candidate must file a report of contributions made by individuals and entities to the Commission. This report is due within three months after the announcement of the election results [act-s94-0].
Who provides security for political rallies and processions and which agencies may assist?

The Commissioner of Police in each State and the Federal Capital Territory is responsible for providing adequate security. The Police may be supported by the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps and any other federal security agency [act-s95-0].
What is the limited role of the Nigerian Police Force and other security agencies during political rallies?

Their role is limited to providing adequate security for the proper and peaceful conduct of rallies and processions. They may act under lawful duty when posted to the event, but cannot perform other functions [act-s95-0].
What kind of language is prohibited in political campaigns?

Political campaigns shall not use abusive language likely to injure religious, ethnic, tribal or sectional feelings. They also shall not employ abusive, intemperate, slanderous or base language designed to provoke violent reaction [act-s96-0].
Which locations are not allowed to be used for political campaigns, rallies, or processions?

Places designated for religious worship, police stations, and public offices shall not be used for political campaigns, rallies, or processions. They also shall not be used to promote, propagate or attack political parties, candidates, or their programmes [act-s96-0].
What penalty does a candidate face for breaking Section 96(5) of the Electoral Act?

Section 96(7) of the Electoral Act provides that a candidate who contravenes any provision of this section is liable to a maximum fine of N5,000,000 or imprisonment for a term of 12 months. Consequently, the penalty for such a candidate is a fine up to N5,000,000 or 12 months of imprisonment [act-s96-1].
What is the punishment for someone who helps a political party violate Section 96(5)?

Section 96(8) states that any person who aids or abets a political party in contravening subsection (5) commits an offence and is liable to a fine of N2,000,000 or imprisonment for three years, or both. Thus, the punishment for such a person is a fine of N2,000,000, three years in prison, or both [act-s96-1].
What penalty does a candidate receive for threatening a voter with force during a campaign?

Section 97(2)(a) of the Electoral Act says that a candidate who threatens a person with force or violence during a campaign is liable to a maximum fine of N5,000,000 or imprisonment for 12 months. Therefore, the penalty for a candidate who makes such threats is a fine up to N5,000,000 or 12 months of imprisonment [act-s97-0].
What fine does a political party face for threatening voters?

Section 97(2)(b) provides that a political party that threatens voters is liable to a fine of N10,000,000 for the first offence and N2,000,000 for any subsequent offence. Hence, the fine for a party that threatens voters is N10,000,000 initially and N2,000,000 for later offences [act-s97-0].
When does the official campaign period start and end according to the Electoral Act?

Section 98(1) of the Electoral Act defines the campaign period as commencing 150 days before polling day and ending 24 hours prior to that day. Accordingly, the official campaign period starts 150 days before polling day and ends 24 hours before polling day [act-s98-0].
What penalty applies to a party that runs a broadcast advertisement in the 24 hours before polling day?

Section 98(2) states that a registered political party which advertises on broadcasting facilities in the 24 hours before polling day commits an offence under this Act. As a result, such a party is liable to a maximum fine of N2,000,000 [act-s98-0].
What rule ensures all political parties receive equal airtime on public electronic media?

Section 99(4) requires that at any public electronic media, equal airtime shall be allotted to all political parties or candidates during prime times at similar hours each day, subject to payment of appropriate fees. Therefore, the rule ensures all parties receive equal airtime during prime times each day [act-s99-0].
What penalty does a public media house face for not giving equal coverage to parties?

Section 99(6)(a) provides that a public media house that contravenes the equal coverage rules is liable to a fine of N2,000,000 in the first instance and N5,000,000 for subsequent convictions. Consequently, the penalty for a public media house that fails to give equal coverage is a fine of N2,000,000 initially and N5,000,000 for later offences [act-s99-0].
What broadcasting activities are prohibited on polling day according to the Electoral Act, 2026?

The Electoral Act, 2026 prohibits any person, print or electronic medium from broadcasting, publishing, advertising or circulating material to promote or oppose a political party or candidate on polling day or the 24 hours immediately preceding it [act-s100-0].
